cards.headline: Growth costs money the founders do not have.
cards.body: A chain with 40 stores wants 400. Building them takes cash the owners cannot spare. So the company sells pieces of itself to strangers, and those strangers become owners. That trade is why the stock market exists.

cards.headline: Going public has a name: the IPO.
cards.body: Initial public offering. The company creates brand-new shares, agrees a price with its bankers, and sells them to investors on the first day of trading. It hands over ownership. It walks away with cash to spend.

cards.headline: The company gets paid once.
cards.body: That IPO cash is the **primary market** — new shares, straight from the company. After that, shares change hands between investors on the **secondary market**. When you buy from another shareholder, the company receives nothing at all.

cards.prompt: You buy 100 shares of a listed company through your broker on a Tuesday. Where does your money actually go?

options.label: To the investor who sold the shares

cards.explanation: Only shares sold **by the company** put cash on its balance sheet. Ordinary trading moves existing shares between investors and leaves the business untouched.

cards.title: Dilution in one move
cards.caption: A founder holding 6 million of 10 million shares owns 60 percent. Issue 2.5 million new shares and the same holding is 48 percent. The slice shrinks; the pie grows.

cards.body: Issuing new shares raises cash but cuts every existing owner's percentage. The word for that shrinking slice is [[1]].
cards.explanation: Dilution is not automatically bad. If the money raised grows the business by more than the slice shrank, existing owners still come out ahead.

cards.headline: A listing also lets early owners cash out.
cards.body: Founders and venture funds hold shares almost nobody could buy. A listing creates a public market for them, so some sell part of their stake. Those are existing shares, so that money goes to the seller, not the business.
Public money comes with a public life. The moment the shares list, a set of obligations arrives and never leaves.

cards.summary: Companies sell shares to turn ownership into cash for growth, and accept dilution and public scrutiny as the price.
bullets: An IPO sells new shares, and the company keeps that cash.
Trades between investors afterwards send the company nothing.
New shares shrink existing stakes, even as the business gets bigger.
A listing buys money and sells freedom — reporting never stops.

cards.insight: A company sells part of itself to buy its future. The cash arrives once; the owners it answers to stay forever.
